note: Statements the coach may give as training and health information. Each one paraphrases its source; keep them short and conservative. Have a qualified professional review before release.

facts.text: Adults should get 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix of the two. More brings further benefits.
facts.source: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020

facts.text: Adults should also do muscle-strengthening activity of moderate or greater intensity that works all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week.
facts.source: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020

facts.text: Adults 65 and older should add varied activity that trains balance and strength on 3 or more days a week, to improve function and prevent falls.
facts.source: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020

facts.text: Some activity is better than none. Limit time spent sitting and replace it with activity of any intensity, even light.
facts.source: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020

facts.text: Beginners do well with 1–3 sets of 8–12 repetitions at a load they can just manage for that many reps, for each major muscle group.
facts.source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults, 2009

facts.text: For maximal strength, trained lifters use heavier loads (about 1–6 repetitions per set) on the main multi-joint lifts, in a planned progression.
facts.source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults, 2009

facts.text: Add load when you can do 1–2 more repetitions than your target on two sessions in a row. Increases of about 2–10% are typical, smaller for upper-body and single-joint lifts.
facts.source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults, 2009

facts.text: Rest 2–3 minutes between sets of heavy multi-joint lifts such as squats and presses, and about 1–2 minutes for lighter or single-joint exercises.
facts.source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults, 2009

facts.text: In trained men, resting 3 minutes between sets led to more strength and muscle growth than resting 1 minute.
facts.source: Schoenfeld BJ et al. J Strength Cond Res, 2016

facts.text: More weekly sets per muscle bring more muscle growth up to a point; about 10 or more hard sets per muscle per week grew more muscle than fewer than 5.
facts.source: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. J Sports Sci, 2017 (meta-analysis)

facts.topic: Training a muscle twice a week
facts.text: Training each muscle group at least twice a week tends to build more muscle than once a week, for the same total work.
facts.source: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Sports Med, 2016 (meta-analysis)

facts.text: Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure; heavier loads build more maximal strength.
facts.source: Schoenfeld BJ et al. J Strength Cond Res, 2017 (meta-analysis)

facts.text: Warm up with 5–10 minutes of light to moderate activity, then a few lighter sets of your first lift before the working sets.
facts.source: ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 11th ed., 2021

facts.text: Short static stretches (under about 60 seconds per muscle) before training have little effect on performance; long holds can briefly reduce strength. A dynamic warm-up is a good default.
facts.source: Behm DG et al. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab, 2016 (review)

facts.text: Moderate intensity is roughly 64–76% of maximum heart rate and vigorous is roughly 77–95%. On the talk test, moderate means you can talk but not sing.
facts.source: ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription; CDC talk test

facts.text: 220 minus age is a rough estimate that can be off by 10 beats or more. Tanaka's formula, 208 minus 0.7 × age, fits adults better on average. A supervised test is the only way to know.
facts.source: Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. J Am Coll Cardiol, 2001

facts.text: Big jumps in weekly running distance are linked to more injuries in new runners. Build up gradually and keep most runs easy.
facts.source: Nielsen RO et al. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 2014

facts.text: For people who train with weights, extra protein helps muscle growth up to about 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day; benefits above that are small. People with kidney disease should ask their doctor.
facts.source: Morton RW et al. Br J Sports Med, 2018 (meta-analysis)

facts.text: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours a night regularly for good health, and recovery from training depends on it.
facts.source: AASM and Sleep Research Society consensus statement, 2015

facts.text: Drink enough to avoid losing more than about 2% of body weight during long or hot sessions, but don't drink far beyond your thirst.
facts.source: ACSM Position Stand: Exercise and Fluid Replacement, 2007

facts.text: Breathe out during the hardest part of each rep. People with high blood pressure or heart disease should avoid holding their breath while lifting.
facts.source: Williams MA et al. AHA Scientific Statement on Resistance Exercise, Circulation, 2007

facts.text: Muscle soreness that peaks 1–3 days after new or harder training is normal and fades. Sharp pain, swelling, or very dark urine after hard exercise are not normal and need medical care.
facts.source: Cheung K, Hume P, Maxwell L. Sports Med, 2003; rhabdomyolysis warning signs

facts.topic: When to check with a doctor first
facts.text: People with known heart, metabolic or kidney disease, or symptoms such as chest discomfort or breathlessness, should get medical clearance before starting or stepping up vigorous exercise.
facts.source: Riebe D et al. ACSM preparticipation screening, Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2015

facts.text: In an uncomplicated pregnancy, about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is recommended, after checking with your obstetric care provider, who should guide any changes.
facts.source: ACOG Committee Opinion 804, 2020
